citations: Billingham & Needham, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 430 (1990) 'The development of travelling waves in a simple isothermal chemical system III. Cubic and mixed autocatalysis' https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspa/article/430/1880/509/16458

notes: With no feed or decay, field 1 is never removed and simply converts field 0 until the substrate is used up; rule 2 only switches 0->1 and never back. The features (one type, largest domain = 1.0) therefore mean the fronts filled the whole torus and every cell was frozen as type 1, not that coarsening happened. full_text:
**My verdict is KNOWN, and I agree with the first pass.** The behaviour is a documented one. What the simulation picked up is the system being driven into a frozen state where every cell is type 1. It's not a genuine emergent pattern.

**What the system is.** The chemistry is the closed cubic autocatalysis A + 2B → 3B, with no feed and no decay of the catalyst. This exact system has been studied directly: "Consider the autocatalytic reaction A + 2B → 3B described by the reaction-diffusion equation", with the reactant decreasing and the catalyst increasing at rate αβ², plus diffusion. In 1D this supports isothermal chemical fronts. The classic analysis (Billingham & Needham, Proc. R. Soc. A 430) states that autocatalytic chemical reactions can support isothermal travelling waves of constant speed and form, and that for pure cubic autocatalysis the wave has, at large times, a constant asymptotic speed. The usual picture is that a localized introduction of the autocatalyst B into a uniform background of substrate A can trigger a travelling reaction front that converts the A-rich state into a B-rich one.

**What the observed features mean.** Without the catalyst decay step, nothing destroys field 1, and the fields don't need a stable pattern to sustain them. Field 1 just keeps converting field 0 until the substrate runs out, so it ends up roughly equal to the local starting total of the two fields. Rule 2 is a one-way switch: once a cell is type 1 it stays type 1. So the cell types simply record where field 1 has ever exceeded 0.8. In these runs the autocatalytic fronts filled the whole torus, field 1 crossed the threshold everywhere, and every cell became type 1. That accounts for both features: one domain covering the whole lattice and one surviving type.

**Why the knock-out evidence doesn't make this a discovery.** Both rules are needed only because one makes the field and the other reads it. With either rule removed nothing ever flips, and the random start stays as it was (largest domain 0.04, two types). The result holds at 4x area and 3x run length because the outcome is guaranteed, not because a pattern is organising itself. None of the things you'd expect from real coarsening appear: no curvature-driven boundaries, no power-law domain growth, no persistent structure.

**One caveat.** Whether field 1 actually reaches 0.8 everywhere depends on the initial total of the two fields. If that total were mostly below 0.8, you'd get a partly flipped pattern frozen in place, which is still an absorbing state. That's a parameter detail, not a new phenomenon.
